title: Algorithmic Complexity of Finding Large Independent Sets in Pair Functions

problemStatement.formal: Given a valid pair function $f : \binom{[n]}{2} \to [n]$ with $f(\{x,y\}) \notin \{x,y\}$, find an independent set $X \subseteq [n]$ (so $f(\{x,y\}) \notin X$ whenever $x,y \in X$) of size $|X| = \Omega(n^{1/2})$, matching $g(n) = \Theta(n^{1/2})$. Is there a $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ (or near-linear) algorithm producing such an $X$, and how hard is the exact maximum-independent-set version?
problemStatement.plain: Erdős Problem #1025 proved that every valid pair function on {1,...,n} has a guaranteed independent set of size g(n) = Θ(n^{1/2}), but only as an existence result. This question asks the algorithmic version: given a specific pair function f, how efficiently can we actually compute an independent set achieving the Ω(n^{1/2}) bound, and how hard is it to find a maximum independent set exactly? The existence proof relies on Spencer's non-constructive probabilistic deletion method, so the challenge is derandomizing it into an efficient deterministic algorithm.
whyMatters: Turning non-constructive extremal existence proofs into efficient algorithms (algorithmic derandomization, as with the Lovász Local Lemma and Moser–Tardos) is a central theme in combinatorics.

Pair functions are a clean special case of set mappings and 3-uniform hypergraph independent sets, so a constructive/complexity result illuminates a whole family of extremal problems; conversely, NP-hardness of the maximum version would sharply delimit tractability.

knownResults: Existence g(n) = Θ(n^{1/2}): Spencer (1972) lower bound plus Conlon–Fox–Sudakov (2016) upper bound, formalized in gallery proof erdos-1025.
Spencer's probabilistic deletion argument is a randomized poly(n) procedure with expected output Ω(n^{1/2}); the method of conditional expectations derandomizes it deterministically.
Erdős–Hajnal's (1958) greedy argument is an explicit deterministic algorithm but only certifies the weaker Ω(n^{1/3}) bound.
Maximum independent set is NP-hard in general (Karp 1972), but the f(x,y) ∉ {x,y} structure does not transfer that hardness automatically — the exact complexity here is open.
references: P. Erdős, A. Hajnal, On the structure of set-mappings, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1958)
J. Spencer, Turán's theorem for k-graphs, Discrete Math. (1972)
N. Alon, J. Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, 4th ed., Wiley (2016)
R. M. Karp, Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems (1972)
